blocks.text: The main bearings of a car engine spin at several thousand revolutions a minute for hundreds of thousands of kilometres, yet the steel journal never touches the bearing shell. It rides on a film of oil only a few hundredths of a millimetre thick, and that film is created by nothing more than the rotation of the shaft itself.

blocks.markdown: A **journal bearing** is a cylindrical bearing in which a shaft (the journal) of diameter $D$ turns inside a sleeve with a slightly larger bore. The difference in radii is the **radial clearance** $c$, typically about 0.001 times the journal diameter. When the shaft is stationary and loaded it rests on the bottom of the bearing in metal-to-metal contact. Once it starts to turn, friction first drags it up the side of the bearing, which is the regime of **boundary lubrication** with high friction and wear.

blocks.title: Hydrodynamic lubrication
blocks.text: In hydrodynamic lubrication the surfaces are fully separated by a fluid film whose pressure is generated by the relative motion itself. The pressure is produced when viscous fluid is dragged into a converging (wedge-shaped) gap, so that a given flow of oil must pass through a smaller and smaller gap and the pressure in the film rises. The load is carried by the integral of this pressure over the film.

blocks.markdown: **How the film forms.** As the speed rises, the rotating journal drags oil, because of its viscosity, round with it into the narrowing gap on the side towards which it has climbed. The pressure in this wedge grows and pushes the journal away from the bearing surface, so the journal lifts and moves to an **eccentric** position, with the centre of the journal displaced by an eccentricity $e$ from the bearing centre, off to the side (not directly beneath the load) and with a minimum film thickness $h_0=c-e$ at the narrowest point. At equilibrium the pressure force exactly balances the load $W$. The key requirements are a viscous liquid, enough relative speed, and a converging gap.

blocks.markdown: **Design parameters.** The load per unit of projected bearing area is the **bearing pressure**, where $L$ is the bearing length and $D$ the journal diameter. The behaviour of the film is governed by the dimensionless **Sommerfeld number**, built from the viscosity $\mu$ (Pa s), the journal speed $N$ (rev/s), the mean pressure $P$ and the clearance ratio $r/c$, where $r=D/2$. A high value means a heavily viscous, fast or lightly loaded bearing, running with a large film thickness and a small eccentricity.

blocks.prompt: A journal of diameter $D=50$ mm runs in a bearing of length $L=50$ mm with radial clearance $c=0.05$ mm. It carries a load $W=2.5$ kN at $N=1500$ rev/min with oil of viscosity $\mu=0.03$ Pa s (typical of warm engine oil). Find the bearing pressure and the Sommerfeld number.

steps.text: Convert the speed and compute the projected area $LD$.

blocks.answer: $P=1.0$ MPa and $S=0.188$. A Sommerfeld number of this order indicates a moderately loaded bearing with a healthy film, which could then be used with design charts to read off eccentricity and friction.

blocks.markdown: **Friction in a lightly loaded bearing: Petroff's law.** For a lightly loaded bearing the journal runs almost concentrically with the bearing. Then the oil film is a thin layer of uniform thickness $c$ sheared between a surface moving at $U=2\pi rN$ and a stationary surface. The shear stress in the Newtonian film is $\tau=\mu U/c$, acting over the area $2\pi rL$ of the journal. The friction force is $F_f=\tau\cdot2\pi rL$ and the torque is $T=F_fr$. This is Petroff's equation, which is exact for zero load and approximate for light loads.

blocks.title: Friction torque and power loss in a lightly loaded bearing
blocks.prompt: A journal of diameter 60 mm in a bearing of length 60 mm has radial clearance $c=0.04$ mm. It runs at 1800 rev/min with oil of viscosity $\mu=0.02$ Pa s and carries a light load of 1.5 kN. Use Petroff's law to find the friction torque, the coefficient of friction and the power loss.

steps.text: Quantities in SI units: $r=0.030$ m, $L=0.060$ m, $c=4\times10^{-5}$ m and $N=30$ rev/s.
Bearing pressure and coefficient of friction from $f=T/(rW)$.
Check by the second Petroff form, $f=2\pi^2(\mu N/P)(r/c)$.
Power loss converts to heat in the oil, so it governs the oil temperature and cooling needed.

blocks.answer: $T=0.96$ N m, $f=0.021$ and the power loss is about 181 W.

blocks.title: Why the film matters
blocks.text: In the hydrodynamic regime the friction coefficient is only about 0.001 to 0.01 and there is no wear, but the film exists only while the speed and viscosity are high enough and the load is not too large. Start-up, shut-down and shock loads fall back to mixed or boundary lubrication, so bearing materials (soft white metal, bronze) and oil supply must be chosen to survive them.

items: Oil viscosity falls with temperature, so power loss heats the oil and lowers the film thickness.
A larger $S$ means smaller eccentricity ratio $e/c$ and a thicker film at the narrowest point.
Increasing the clearance lowers friction but also lowers the load capacity of the film.
Petroff's law ignores the eccentricity, so it underestimates friction at high loads.

points: A hydrodynamic film forms when the rotating journal drags viscous oil into a converging wedge; the resulting pressure lifts and eccentrically positions the journal so that it floats.
Bearing pressure is $P=W/(LD)$ on the projected area, and $S=(r/c)^2\mu N/P$ with $N$ in rev/s is the governing dimensionless group.
Petroff's law gives friction torque $T=4\pi^2\mu r^3LN/c$ and a friction coefficient $f=2\pi^2(\mu N/P)(r/c)$ for light loads.
Power loss $2\pi NT$ is dissipated as heat in the oil; start-up and low-speed operation are in boundary or mixed lubrication.

questions.stem: Which three conditions are needed to build a hydrodynamic film in a journal bearing?

options.text: A viscous fluid, relative motion of the surfaces and a converging gap
An oil pump, a hard bearing surface and a very small clearance
High pressure supplied externally, a thick film and a hard journal
A low-viscosity fluid, a stationary shaft and parallel surfaces

questions.correctOptionText: A viscous fluid, relative motion of the surfaces and a converging gap

distractorRationale.a: Correct: viscous drag carries the fluid into a wedge, building pressure.
distractorRationale.b: A pump is not needed for hydrodynamic action, and clearance alone does not create pressure.
distractorRationale.c: External pressure describes a hydrostatic bearing.
distractorRationale.d: Without motion and a wedge, no pressure is generated.

questions.explanation: In a hydrodynamic bearing the pressure comes from the shaft's own motion dragging viscous oil into a narrowing gap. A parallel gap would produce no net load capacity.

questions.stem: A heavily loaded journal bearing is just starting from rest. Which lubrication regime is present at this moment?

options.text: Boundary lubrication, with asperity contact and high friction
Hydrodynamic lubrication with a thick film
Hydrostatic lubrication
Elastohydrodynamic lubrication of a rolling contact

questions.correctOptionText: Boundary lubrication, with asperity contact and high friction

distractorRationale.a: Correct: no film exists until enough speed is achieved.
distractorRationale.b: The film is built only after the speed rises.
distractorRationale.d: EHL concerns rolling contacts such as gear teeth and rolling bearings.

questions.explanation: At rest there is no relative motion to pump oil into the wedge, so the surfaces touch. This is why bearing materials must tolerate rubbing during start-up and why friction coefficients are highest in this regime.

questions.stem: All else being equal, the load on a journal bearing is increased. What happens to the Sommerfeld number and to the journal's eccentricity?

options.text: $S$ decreases and the eccentricity increases (thinner minimum film)
$S$ increases and the eccentricity decreases
$S$ is unchanged because it does not contain the load
$S$ decreases and the minimum film gets thicker

questions.correctOptionText: $S$ decreases and the eccentricity increases (thinner minimum film)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: S is inversely proportional to the pressure and a more heavily loaded bearing runs more eccentric.
distractorRationale.b: S falls with load, not rises.
distractorRationale.c: S contains P = W/(LD) in the denominator.
distractorRationale.d: A smaller S corresponds to a thinner film, not a thicker one.

questions.explanation: $S=(r/c)^2\mu N/P$ and $P$ rises with $W$, so $S$ falls. A low Sommerfeld number corresponds to a high eccentricity ratio and a small minimum film thickness, hence a greater risk of metal contact.

questions.stem: For a lightly loaded journal bearing, the radial clearance is doubled with all other quantities held constant. According to Petroff's equation, what happens to the friction torque?

options.text: It halves
It doubles
It quarters
It is unchanged

distractorRationale.b: Torque falls with more clearance because the film is thicker and the shear rate lower.
distractorRationale.c: A factor of four would need T proportional to 1/c^2.
distractorRationale.d: T clearly depends on c through the shear stress mu U/c.

questions.explanation: From $T=4\pi^2\mu r^3LN/c$ the torque is inversely proportional to $c$, because a thicker film has a smaller velocity gradient. The price is a reduced load capacity and a lower Sommerfeld number effect via $(r/c)^2$.

questions.stem: A shaft of diameter 40 mm runs in a bearing 60 mm long and supports a load of 4 kN. What is the bearing pressure used in the Sommerfeld number?

options.text: 1.67 MPa
0.53 MPa
3.33 MPa

distractorRationale.b: 0.53 MPa uses the curved surface area pi D L instead of the projected area.
distractorRationale.c: 3.33 MPa results from dividing by only half of the projected area.
distractorRationale.d: 0.0017 MPa results from a units slip, dividing newtons by mm squared and then scaling by 10^-3 instead of 1.

questions.explanation: Journal bearing pressure is defined on the projected area $LD=2400$ mm$^2$, so $P=4000/2400=1.67$ MPa. The curved area would give a smaller number that is not used by the design charts.

questions.stem: A journal of diameter 75 mm and length 100 mm carries a radial load of 9 kN. Find the bearing pressure on the projected area in MPa.
questions.explanation: The projected area is $LD=100\times75=7500$ mm$^2$. Then $P=W/(LD)=9000/7500=1.20$ MPa.

questions.stem: A journal bearing has $D=40$ mm, radial clearance $c=0.05$ mm, bearing pressure $P=2.0$ MPa, oil viscosity $\mu=0.025$ Pa s and speed $N=20$ rev/s. Find the Sommerfeld number (dimensionless).

A lightly loaded journal of diameter 40 mm and length 40 mm runs in a bearing with radial clearance $c=0.04$ mm at 2400 rev/min. The oil viscosity is $\mu=0.015$ Pa s. Use Petroff's law to find the power loss in W.
questions.explanation: With $r=0.020$ m and $N=40$ rev/s the friction torque is $T=4\pi^2\times0.015\times0.020^3\times0.040\times40/(4\times10^{-5})=0.189$ N m. The power loss is $2\pi NT=2\pi\times40\times0.189=47.6$ W.

questions.stem: Explain how a hydrodynamic oil film is formed and sustained in a journal bearing, describing what happens from start-up to steady running and why the journal settles in an eccentric position.
markingGuide: At rest the journal is in contact at the bottom of the bearing (boundary lubrication).
On rotation, viscous drag carries oil into the gap; the journal climbs the bearing surface and the gap becomes a converging wedge.
The oil flow rate through a smaller gap must be accommodated by pressure rise; the film pressure builds up in the converging region.
The resultant of the pressure force balances the load and lifts the journal clear of the bearing; the film is at its thinnest ($h_0=c-e$) after the point of maximum pressure.

The journal is displaced sideways and eccentric, not directly under the load, because the pressure distribution and wedge geometry require a line of centres offset from the load line; increasing speed or viscosity or reducing load makes the journal more concentric.
questions.explanation: Hydrodynamic pressure is generated by the wedge geometry, which exists only because of the journal eccentricity. At higher speed the journal rises towards concentricity.

questions.stem: State Petroff's equation for the friction torque in a lightly loaded journal bearing, outline its derivation including assumptions, and explain what the Sommerfeld number represents and how it is used to judge whether a bearing is likely to run hydrodynamically.
markingGuide: Assumption: concentric journal, uniform film thickness $c$, Newtonian oil with constant viscosity, no end leakage effects, light load.
Surface speed $U=2\pi rN$; shear stress $\tau=\mu U/c$.
Friction force $\tau\cdot2\pi rL$ and torque $T=4\pi^2\mu r^3LN/c$; power loss $=2\pi NT$.
Friction coefficient $f=2\pi^2(\mu N/P)(r/c)$, showing dependence on $\mu N/P$.

Sommerfeld number $S=(r/c)^2\mu N/P$ is a dimensionless group that fixes the eccentricity ratio and the minimum film thickness for a given $L/D$; large $S$ indicates a thick film, small $S$ a thin film and risk of contact, so design charts relate $S$ to $h_0/c$, friction and flow.
questions.explanation: Petroff's law gives a quick estimate of friction at light load, while the Sommerfeld number carries the full film behaviour including eccentricity. Both depend on the same group $\mu N/P$.
